Q: Printing 9 lines counting from 0-9 not working A:

You are going to want to use for loops. Depending on if you want an int or string to print out there are two ways I can think of doing this while being as literal as possible about the answer.

If all you need is to print the numbers to the screen a string should suffice.

def countdown():
for i in range(0,9):        #Iterate for 9 lines
    x=""                    #Using string x
    for j in range(0,10):   #Iterate through numbers 0-9 which is actually ten digits
        x += str(j)         #convert the int j to a string and add it to string x
    print(x)

If your trying to output an int convert the string to int an before printing.

def countdown():
for i in range(0,9):        #Iterate for 9 lines
    x=""                    #Using string x
    for j in range(0,10):   #Iterate through numbers 0-9 which is actually ten digits
        x += str(j)         #convert the int j to a string and add it to string x        
    y = int(x)              #convert the string x to int y
    print(y)

In either case your shell should print this:

>>> countdown()
0123456789
0123456789
0123456789
0123456789
0123456789
0123456789
0123456789
0123456789
0123456789

You were attempting to use a list which could achieve a similar result but not what you asked for.

Q: Join to only the "latest" record with t-sql A:

Use OUTER APPLY, if you want it behave like a LEFT OUTER JOIN.

SELECT *
FROM tableA A
OUTER APPLY (SELECT TOP 1 * 
             FROM tableB B
             WHERE A.ID = B.TableAID
             ORDER BY B.RowDate DESC) as B

Otherwise CROSS APPLY, if records from Table A must match at least one record from Table B, and therefore should behave like and INNER JOIN

Q: Alter all tables postgres set owner A: 
UPDATE pg_class
SET relowner = 'username_you_want'::RegRole
WHERE
        relnamespace = 'schema_you_want'::RegNamespace
    AND relkind IN ('r','p') /* Since original post said "tables". */
    AND … … /* Whatever other condition you like */
;

Be sure to know exactly which objects will be affected, before running! Check with e.g.

SELECT relkind, relname, relowner::RegRole
WHERE relowner <> 'username_you_want'::RegRole
  AND … /* Everything from the UPDATE command's WHERE clause */
;

Note, added 2026jul17: if you're going through psql, by all means use the \gexec trick as others explain above. This approach is for when \gexec is not available to you. (Thanks to @Bergi for reminding me to mention that!)

Q: JAXB chokes on UTF-16 XML A:

Running xmlstarlet fo on the document produced the following error:

/path/to/document.xml:1.38: Document labelled UTF-16 but has UTF-8 content

In conclusion, org.xml.sax.SAXParseException with the error message Content is not allowed in prolog is fairly unspecific and in some cases misleading.

While usually it indicates that illegal extra characters (including nonprinting ones) were encountered before the root element, it may also indicate something completely different – such as the XML prolog specifying an encoding which does not match the actual encoding.

Q: In Bash in a macOS environment, how can extract a sentence before a word and after a word in an XML document? A:

Here's two bash examples:

webout='<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-16"?><interface-response><Command>SETDNSHOST</Command><Language>eng</Language><ErrCount>1</ErrCount><errors><Err1>Passwords do not match</Err1></errors><ResponseCount>1</ResponseCount><responses><response><Description>Passwords do not match</Description><ResponseNumber>304156</ResponseNumber><ResponseString>Validation error; invalid ; password</ResponseString></response></responses><Done>true</Done><debug><![CDATA[]]></debug></interface-response>'


sed -n  "s:.*<Description>\(.*\)</Description>.*:\1:p" <<< $webout


grep -oP '(?<=<Description>).*(?=</Description>)' <<< $webout

To be honest, the second command (grep) is using a syntax that I'm not too familiar with (I just picked it up here: https://unix.stackexchange.com/questions/13466/can-grep-output-only-specified-groupings-that-match ).

However, when you are parsing XML, you are better off not using regex but rather an xml parser.

Here's a third option using an XML parse (xmllint):

xmllint --xpath '//Description/text()' -  <<< $webout

Note: I had to change utf-16 to utf-8 to make xmllint happy.

After I read comments and other answers, on this page, I discovered that iconv is the command for converting from UTF-8 to UTF-16. Here's an improved version:

xmllint --xpath '//Description/text()' <(  iconv -f utf-8  -t utf-16 <<< $webout )

Q: Remove multiple occurrences of similar lines except the last A:

You are essentially doing a conditional slice on a file stream when there is a break between a match condition and a no match condition and wanting the last match from a string of matches.

Ruby is exquisite for these types of uses.

A kinda awky looking Ruby:

ruby -e '
p, last = /^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}/, nil
ARGF.each_line(chomp: true){ |line|
    if p.match?(line)
        last = line
        next
    end
    if last
        puts last
        last = nil
    end
    puts line
}
puts last if last' file

Or more idiomatically:

ruby -e '
    p = /^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}/
    ARGF.each_line(chomp: true)
        .slice_when { |a, b| a.match?(p) != b.match?(p) }
        .each { |g| puts g.first.match?(p) ? g.last : g }' file

(This one is handy if you wanted a more complex relationship of the match block...)

Either one prints:

important information 1
important information 2
2026-07-10T11:15:09.647148-04:00     <-- keep
important information 3
important information 4
important information 5
2026-07-10T11:15:12.662378-04:00     <-- keep
important information 6
important information 7
2026-07-10T11:15:18.232970-04:00     <-- keep
important information 8
2026-07-10T11:30:22.788192-04:00     <-- keep
important information 9
important information 10
important information 11

The first only holds a max of 2 lines in memory (the current input in $_ and last) and the second will hold the max of each run of matches in an array. So if you have a 10 million line run of matches use the first...

Alternately, you could use POSIX sed:

sed -E '
/^[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}/ { 
    # match block: hold it, flush only on last line, then skip the else
    h
    $!d
    b end
}
# else kinda. do this block with no match up to end marker
{   
    # swap pattern and hold space
    x

    # print last match if there is one and then blank the space
    /^$/!p
    s/.*//

    # swap to print non matching line
    x
} 
:end' file
(same output)

Or Perl:

perl -ne '
if (/^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}/) { $last = $_; next }
if ($last) { print $last; undef $last }
print;
END { print $last if $last }' file
(same output)

Or as jhnc mentioned in comments:

perl -ne '$a = /^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}/ ? $_ : !print$a,$_' file
#                                          ^ needed to negate $a 
#                                          'cause print returns 1 on success

Which is a very Perlly golf use of the ternary. Which you could also do in Ruby (print does not need to be negated in this case):

ruby -ne '$a = /^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}/ ? $_ : print($a,$_)' file
